blocks.x: I think the tape is turning now.
Uh-huh.
What did you say your name was?
Lawrence Ingram. Yeah.

And my name is Dick Allen, and we're doing an interview today in the Seminar Room 2, the Howard Tilton Library, Tulane University. What is today's date? Is it September the 20... I don't know. 27, 1965 I think. Anyway it's Monday. So, I wanted to ask you a few things about jazz in Sweden and New Orleans, if there's any relationship between the two. When were you born by the way?
1944. Mm-hmm. 5th June.
The 5th of June, 1944. Yeah. And where were you born?
Stockholm.
And that's in Sweden.
That's the main town. I see.
When did you get interested in jazz?

That was through my father and my brother. My father played bandwagon in a jazz band in the 30s. And my brother started playing around the early 50s. So they used to have rehearsal in our home. And I used to start picking on bandwagon. That's where I started. Then I started taking piano lessons when I was seven years old, classical stuff. And I was doing that when I was about 15. That's when I started playing jazz.
Do you think that playing classical music hurts your playing at all?
No, it couldn't hurt me now because I can't play enough, you know, that stuff no more. Yeah. I can't read music very well no more.
You forgot at all. Yeah.

Well I can't read but I can't really play. I can figure out melody lines and stuff like that. I learned the most, piano I learned, but bandwagon and clarinet and stuff I learned all by myself, without taking any other lessons at all.
How many instruments do you play now?
Tell me. I play piano, bandwagon, guitar, clarinet, saxophone, and mandolin.
What kind of saxophone?
It's alto saxophone.
Alto. The tape machine is making a little scraping noise. Anyway, what kind of music did your father play? I never did quite understand about that.

Yeah, he played in what you would call fast-forward style a little, that kind of music. They had trumpet, saxophone, piano, bandwagon, bass I guess was a drum. They played like, you know, all these songs from the 30s, Evergreen, all this stuff. It's not really a jazz band, it was more a dance band. But he knew most of the tunes that I used to play too.
And your brother, what kind of music did he play?
He was a Dixlam piano player. He was self-thought. He never took any lessons.
And what was his name?
His name is Tommy. Tommy.
And is he older than you then?

Yeah, yeah. He's 27 I think now. Yeah, 26, 27. But he just quit playing. He's married for a couple of years ago. He quit playing quite early by the way. He quit playing sometime in the late 50s because he didn't like that everybody liked rock and roll music. He figured there was no use of playing no more.
Well what about the Swedish musicians? You mentioned earlier they quit playing a lot of them when they get married?
Yeah.
Why is that?

Because all the places where they play it's only young people. Where I play for example, and it's getting more and more like that now, but when my brother was playing, he also played with people in his own age. There wasn't, nobody was old at that 25 for example. That's, you hardly ever see anyone. Mostly they are around 18, that age. And you feel kind of all in sitting playing with these people. You don't get the same joy out of it. Just playing with them. And another thing about playing jazz in Sweden is, I mean traditional jazz, you only play for dancing. Maybe concerts now and then. You play for dancing all the time.
Well what do most people like in the way of music over there?
Well they like the Beatles nowadays.
So they like a lot of the rock and roll or whatever you want to call it?
Oh yeah.
Most of the young people.
Yeah. I mean it's getting worse and worse for jazz music now. It's been getting worse and worse since the 1940s and 49 or 48 when they started playing.
They started having Swedish jazz bands about that time?

Well they had bands earlier but it was more like dance bands. It wasn't that much jazz bands. In the middle of 44 as it said in that book. That was one of the first jazz bands. I never heard anything of that recording. The only first, the earliest recording I ever heard of jazz, Swedish jazz tradition is 49. Was that the Hapcats? No that was not the Hapcats. I was with the... I was with the... I can't remember that. It was called Gravo, right? Gravo, right? He had a girl sing in that tour. He sang like... I had a Corks and Maraine and stuff like that. That was the type of music they played. King Oliver and stuff like that. They never... They didn't play any of those... just Frank Jones and stuff. Just Lois and nothing like that. Played like Oliver and Armstrong and Kiddoi.
Do you know the girl's name who sang?
Britta something. Britta Lindahl?
Yeah, that's it.
She moved over here I think.
Oh, I didn't know that. Yeah. Yeah, she's on page 28 of this book of... Oh. ...Rollanda. Uh... I can't pronounce it. Ungdomens Jatskalender or something? Yeah. How do you say it?
Jazz calendar.
Yeah? I see. What does it say on the top?
That's the... The Youth Jazz Calendar. Oh. Say it in Swedish for me. Ungdomens Jatskalender.
I see. Yeah.
But that record, that wasn't the original record I heard. It was originally put out two years ago or one year.
It must have been since about 1950 or 51 since I've heard the Hepcats.
Hmm?
But as I remember they sounded very much like the Kid Ory band.
Yeah.
Jack Lindstrom sounded like Mud Carey then, huh?
Yeah. But Lindstrom nowadays, he plays mostly like Armstrong nowadays. Mm-hm. And his band is kind of modernized.
Mm-hm.

But he's still playing. He... Last time I heard him play was in... The Jazz Festival they had two years ago in South Sweden. Conk Bates was there and Niklas was there. Mm-hm. He was playing there then. That was the last time I heard his band. We was there too. We were all band and played. It was a Danish band, you know, kind of band from all over the world.
Who was the Danish band? Yeah.
Papa Boo. Papa Boo. And I think it was Henrik Johansson or something. Yeah. Maybe Papa Bernie too. I'm not sure.
Well what band do you play with now? We're jumping around so much.
The band I play now is called Imperial Band. We've been playing for about three years.
Who's the leader?

I am the leader. But now I'm gone so now the Clarence player is the leader. It's not really... It's a leader. It's not really a leader in the band. Just everybody is a leader. The leader... The only thing with the leader is that he gets the jobs and pays the musics. That's the only... There's no musical leader at all. There's nobody saying now we play this tune.
Well who's in your band? What are the names of the people?

Well it's Christer Fellas on the trumpet. Yeah. And Orian Selin on the planet. Ralph Bandler, trombone. And Ingmar Wistrand, Banyo. I don't know what the new bass player is. They change bass player now. And drum is Chris Rolson.
Who was your bass player before?
He bass player. The last one we had him called Otter Sörman, which is a youngster just came. He had started playing a year ago. He was over in England all this summer.
Oh yeah. We should write these names down so we have the correct spellings later. Yeah. But it's so hard for me to understand. But there are other bands like yours that play on the style?

Right now it's just about, in Stockholm there's only two bands I would say who play this kind of music we play. I mean there are a lot of traditional bands, but most of them play more modern style. They play a type of Eddie Conner style, something like that, most of the bands. But we had only two bands, his imperial band is one called Original Optimus Orchestra, which Rolf plays in.
Rolf Waldo.

Yeah. He has the band. I'm playing piano with that band when I'm home too, because his piano player had left just about a year ago. I see. So I play in two bands. But he don't play often because, as I say, he's married. And then the guys in his band, they are a lot older than the guys in my band. They started out way before me. They are more involved in other things.

Yeah, well, the Swedish women I've heard about. Yeah, yeah. It's a great American mythology. But no, seriously, what style do you characterize your band as? Do you have any particular influences? Yeah.

When we started playing, the musicians were in a very different style, all of them. But after a while, it sounded similar to a Bunk Johnson band, I would say. And now later, it changed a little. But Kleiner played, he played more like Bonner's style, you know. He used to play more like Lewis. It changed a little more. We played, we kind of played that style with very few solos. We didn't even play piano over the door in the beginning. And we had the drummer, he played strictly Baby Don's style. Just getting that. But that's our band. The Rolf band is very different. They played the late, just Louis style. You know, more cymbal drums and more and more kind of modern style in some ways I would say.
The modern New Orleans.
Yeah. There's a big difference. Yeah, New Orleans today I would say, more like that.
More like they play Preservation Hall?
Yeah, more like they do that. We don't play like that at all in the band I play with.
I see. I don't know, I keep jumping around from one thing to another and asking about it. But what was your first band you played with?

Oh, that was another band. First I played with my brother. But that was just very irregular. No, just now and then I mean. Did the band have a name? No, I guess they had a name. When I came in my brother almost quit playing already. So he just played a few jobs that came up with friends, more private jobs. Then I used to go with them and play band with him. Then I played with a band called the Snakes or something like that. I don't remember. I think it was the Snakes. That was a modern Dixland band. Some of the guys in the band I played more than jazz. Some of them even professional. There I played with them for a year and then I joined this band.
And then who is your own personal favorite, influences?

Well, I guess, what it most sounds like is probably like Elton Bonner. But it's not that he's my favorite piano player. It's just that I think it fits in good with the band I play. And it's simply, I think it's the style that I can come closer to. True, I don't have the good technique. And he don't have the good technique either, I think.
Who would you name as your favorite piano player?
Jimmy Jansen.
James B. You like him, huh?
James B. Johnson. Is that who you mean? No, no, I mean Jimmy Jansen. Jansen.
Who did he play with?
Play on his own, yeah. You know who he's Jansen. Oh, Yancy! Yeah, yeah.
Oh, yeah.
That's my favorite piano player.
I love his playing.
Yeah, I think he's great. But I mean I couldn't play that in the band. No, you couldn't just play blues.
I love him because he's so simple.
Yeah, exactly.
But nobody can play like him. It's so easy.
It's so much machine if you try to play like him. Yeah.

Well, he had that time and that feeling and that touch. If you don't have that you've just lost everything. It's so amazing that anybody could play that simple and get so much music out of it. He just had so much inside of him I guess it comes out. Since you've been in New Orleans, well what happened when you came to New Orleans? I'll put it that way. You came alone?

Yeah, I hitchhiked from here, from Chicago. I came here in the morning and I saw Jeffy. I went down to Preservation Island and I saw him. I think it was a Saturday because that guitar player was playing like that. What is his name? Babe Stovall. Yeah, he was playing. I knowed him through a radio program from what I learned before. So I went in there and I was there. They had a jam session after that, which I also was with and I played a few songs. I sat in with Johnny Wicks and Raymond Burke. And since then Johnny Wicks have wanted to play with me. We played a similar style in some ways. He thinks so anyway.
Was that the time when Bob Green was here?
Yeah, exactly.
They were making a record that day?
Yeah, the next day they made the record. I wasn't there then. Oh, I see. Then in the evening I heard Kit Homs Band was the first band I heard. I wasn't very impressed at all.
Why not?

I don't know why. It didn't sound good to me. Mostly because I got hung up on the piano player. I think I didn't like him at all. No, I like him better. Who is he? It's Charlie Hamilton. Oh, yeah. I didn't dig him at all. I was, after listening to Joe Yamp, which I also like a lot, I just couldn't stand his playing.
Do you think he fits a Kit Thomas Band? No, I don't think so.
Maybe, I think he fits not too bad. I just didn't like him at all the first time. And Kit Thomas didn't sound as good either, I think. So.

Yeah. Let me check the tape and see if it's recording. Hold on. Okay. What's your name? It's a bit of Franka. Okay, she's going to take over running the machine and free me for thinking, I hope, and asking questions. All right, let's see, we were talking about the change in the piano player. Yeah. Kid Thomas. Yeah. And you say you like Charlie Hamilton now.

I like him better after hearing him. Why? First when I heard him I thought he plays too much all over the piano to fit in Kit Thomas Band. But that was mainly because I heard Hugh James before he plays very simple I guess. I think that's the reason why I thought he didn't fit in.
And you said Thomas wasn't playing so good then?
No, well he was playing out of tune a lot when I heard him last night. And I didn't like that too much.
Did you hear any other bands since you've been here?

Oh yeah, I've been, I would say I've been at preservation almost every night. I've also been to Dixler and all, I've been to Harmony and I've been with the Sheik at a few jobs. And at the parties and I played some parades. So I had a session too with this Japanese fellow, a recording session.
Hiramatsu, Toshiki Hiramatsu.
Yeah.
What about the Harmony and what was that like?
Oh it was just dance music. It wasn't really jazz. The only thing that sounded any good was Sing, the piano player. Sing Melo? Yeah, he sounded pretty good.
Yeah, I like his playing too.

Actually he sounded similar to Alton Pennell in some ways. Except that's when he was playing with the melody with a few things between. But when he tried to play a real solo, it kind of broke close too much. When he did what? When he tried to play an improviser all through a solo. He just couldn't keep it together. It didn't sound very well. I see.
Well, what about the recording session? Whose band was that?

I think it was recorded under the Milbarn's name. But I mean it wasn't the band really. Well the same band had actually been recorded before by Mills, Ken Mills I think. Or maybe Barry Martin. But that was just Barry Martin.
Oh Barry.
I think so. I'm not sure what they said in the band. But we didn't. That wasn't the reason we didn't put it together that way because we asked for- I'm going to turn it off, excuse me.
Before we interrupted, we were talking about Emil Barnes and the recording session. And you said it may have been recorded by Barry Martin before another time. What band was it? Who was that?

There was Eddie Richardson was on trumpet and he sang a few songs. Emil Barnes, Clarenheten, No Trombone Play, Femme Bourgeois, Banyol, Sylvester Henry Bass, Henry Revelle, and the piano player came in later on. His name is Sammy Hopkins.
I see. Well, how did the music go? Pretty well, huh? Oh, pretty bad.

Pretty bad. Mainly because they didn't have any rehearsal. It was supposed to be rehearsal but Tashaki had to leave the next day or the same night so he didn't have time. It would have sounded a lot better if Sammy Hopkins would have been there. Because he was actually out to practice a lot. He couldn't do much. It would have sounded better without him, I think. And another drummer, this drummer didn't fit in very well, yeah. He was swinging but didn't fit in the style. He couldn't play on the snare drum or nothing like that.
Who are some of your favorite musicians that you've heard here, say on bass?
Sylvester Henry I think is the best.
You think he's the best of all the bass players?
Yeah, well I've heard since I came here.
Yeah.

Yeah, I think he's the best. But I only heard him at this session but his sound is very good. And Richard I think is very good too. I like him very much. And D. De De Pair, very good. What is this guy? There isn't too many good musicians around the world.
What about saxophones? Like any of them?
Handy was there playing one night. It's very good. John Handy.
Yeah.
He's good. I would like to hear Pulo Braun from saxophone. I think he's very good. But he refused to play. I wonder why.
I don't know.

I asked him to bring him and funny enough also, Alan Jaffe asked him too. But he won't bring it down. He don't think that people would like it. They say he still can play it. They say he can play it if he laid off 15 years age. He could play it. But you don't want to go and love it. It's a shame because the way he played a clown is it's just a saxophone style. It's nothing else.
Yeah, his tone has changed too.
Yeah, well his clarinet, he don't have, his clarinet tune is kind of a classic tune.
Yeah. He got trained and everything. Are there any clarinet players you've heard here who you like?
Why, I like George Lois. Though he don't sound as good as he used to. And I like Pulo Braun actually. I like his ideas but I don't like his tone. Who else is playing clarinet?
Can John Handy play clarinet?
Yeah, he can play clarinet. But as all saxophone players he's got a bad tone. He always got a bad tone. I like me boss. I still like me boss. Though he can't play too much.
But he's very much out of practice.
Yeah. Well he hasn't played in nine months when he had a session.
You know when we went to see him on Saturday to visit him after the flood and everything, he was talking about his ideas about music. Do you agree with him at all?
Yeah.
What do you think?

I think that the way he's, like he said, we should play more soft and we should play more slow. I think that is right. Gorman told me the same thing. When I was always, he told me exactly the same thing. When the clarinet play in low reggae, the band should, so they should play not too loud. I don't like the way they play at the Preservation Hall. There's tunes and drums, solas, bass, band, and so it's all the time. It's awful boring.
What about Gorman now? He was organizing a band just before he died.
Yeah, he told me he was organizing a band. He also told me who was in the band. But I can't remember it. I only remember Andy Anderson.
I saw Anderson Sunday and I asked him about it, but we didn't have time. The band's time was not.
I asked him too, later on. And he told me it was right that he had a band. But since the hurricane, he hadn't heard anything from Gorman.
I think he told me they had three or four rehearsals. Yeah.

Well Gorman told me he was going to try to get the band out in the country and play, because he knows some places like, outside of New Orleans, where he could get out. But he was very enthusiastic about it. I don't think he would turn out so good. He would think it would make a hit or something.
I didn't ask you anything about Dixieland Hall yet.

Yeah, I've been there a few times. I listened to Howard. I never listened to the other band. I've just been there, paying attention, because I already heard them on records and it sounds bad enough not to be worse to go in there.
Papa French, I guess.
Yeah, I can't stand there. Howard isn't doing too much either.
What does he play like now?
He plays kind of the melody on the trough, even on solos. Sometimes it comes out something better. Not much.
You think trumpet players ought to play more than the melody?

Well, actually he don't need to play more than melody if he has some other good guys in the band when he don't have it. Just there is no idea going there to listen to Kid Howard, because you hear him only play the melody and nobody else doing anything good. Otherwise it's good not to try to play the melody a lot. I think that's very good.
Well, what about the other places on Bourbon Street, like the Red Garter?
Well, the Red Garter. Yeah, I heard the stuff there. I've been there when I went to the Sunday afternoon. And I was calling for girls to play. And now when yours, Lewis.
George Lewis has just taken the place of Jim Lipsman's band there.
Yeah, the Clannotella was fired from then. That's why the whole band left.
And I think they went to your father's mustache.
Yeah, right.
What did that band play like?
Well, it was kind of a modern Dixman band, I would say. Both Ervin Alcon and Fregassoll played more modern than they usually do.
Did they sound like Eddie Connan's band, or did they sound like Turk Martin?
Well, they didn't sound like any particular band. It's just more modern style in some way.
Dixieland?
Yeah, more Dixieland style in India. Alcon didn't change so much, but Fregassof was the one that changed more.
What about George Lewis's band there? Do they play the same as they played Preservation Hall?

Yeah, I would say so. But they don't have the same line-up. They have a different piano player and they don't have a bass. Actually, he sounds better with the white piano player. It's an old Yardhunt. Yeah, he plays better than all the others, I would say. But the others can't keep the right chords and the right beat all the time. None of the guys in the band likes Eddie Connan. I don't know why they play with that. Because they always ask me to sit in and they always say that she's bad all the time. And she don't like to play it either.
She seems soft to me. She doesn't like to play New Orleans music? No.

She wants to play modern stuff. She plays with her son. She has a band with her son, so they play more modern jazz. Her favorite music is Latin music. She told me. She said it's just like work nowadays. It's a drag to play it and it's too much hard work, she said. Playing this chord. She plays a lot of wrong chords also. Like when George plays Pagano Street Blues, she just leaves out two chords in it. It sounds very funny. George don't like it either because he's kind of blowing in her ear and trying to make it the right chord.
But at that other place they had Sim Zimmerman on piano, Dave Oxley, Jack Willis and Williamson.
It's another trumpet, yeah. I don't usually play with him. With the horn. Yeah. Yeah.
So that makes a difference in the sound.
Yeah, it's not too much different, but it's kind of better. It sounds better really. I think that might be because the sound of the hall is better there. The sound in the room is much better.
Is the audience any different in the two-fold?
Well, the audience in the garden is horrible.
What kind of people are they?
I don't know. They are drunkards and that kind of people. You know you are that too. They were screaming at all. They were screaming for the saints all the time. All the banjo tunes.
They were asking the band.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
It was all kind of corny musicians.
Oh yeah, yeah. It wasn't the same with the sound before when I was there too. With these kind of people screaming.
They had George's sound before?
Yeah. He's been there two weeks.
He's been there two weeks, I see. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
has a brass band. I only play with it once or twice.
What instruments?
I play bass drum.
Oh, you play bass drum too?
Yeah.
I see.
I actually played when George Lewis was there in February. We was meeting him at the airport with a brass band. That's his recorder too. Roll by the tape with him. It was too bad you didn't hear it.
Yeah. Have you had a lot of New Orleans musicians coming to Sweden?
Well, George Lewis is coming there quite often. Albert Nicholas, Edmund Hall, you know. Otherwise it's mostly Chris Bob and Papa Boo coming there. They'd very seldom bring in the-
Trap bands.
Yeah. A lot of modern jazz of course. Very lot of modern jazz.
Is modern jazz more popular?
Yeah. It's very popular in Sweden. I guess it's more popular than any other country in Europe. I see. And there's also more modern jazz musicians in Sweden than in other countries.
Well, how do the traditional musicians make it then? They don't make it. They just play
for the fun.
You don't get much money or what?

No. We make- sometimes we make money like when I played at the jazz festival two years ago and we went- this Christmas we went on a tour to Denmark for 14 days with the band. Then we make some money. Otherwise we make money when we go out on the countryside. Not in Stockholm. In Stockholm you don't make no money at all no more. They all want modern jazz? Well they don't want pop music. Modern jazz they don't make it either. The jazz make it when they play in restaurants. They never play for dancing more than jazz. So. OK. OK.
I'd say this is Lars Edergren, is that him? Yeah, that's it.
Roughly.
Roughly, yeah. You better ask him. Real two September 27th.
Actually, my name is Lars Edergren. Lars Edergren. Yeah, it's two names. Eder is my father's name.
Oh. That's your full name, but people just call you Lars.
Yeah, they call me Lars.
And it's September 27th, 1965. So Mrs. Franca has just left. I'm going to raise her name. We're in the tape machine. We were talking about some of the German bands you mentioned. Yeah, yeah.

Where did you hear them? I heard, let's see, mainly I heard them on records actually. I met a few musicians. I don't think I heard any full band in person. I just met a few musicians and played with them. I met one in England when I was playing with little Wicky Smith's band in England. There was a German piano player over there who was from town near, called Wuppertown, very near Düsseldorf. I also visited them later.
Where have you been in Europe? You've been to Sweden, of course.
Yeah, I've been to Denmark, Germany, Belgium, France, Spain, England, Scotland, and Wales. I heard music in different places.
I heard music in England, of course. England and Scotland and Wales, I heard music in different bands.
And I heard music in France, not in Spain, not in Belgium.
I mean New Orleans style bands.

Well, traditional jazz I would say. I heard, it was very funny because about two years ago when I was in Paris, it was stupid for me not to pick up the name. I met an old New Orleans musician, saxophone player and piano player, who told me, which I don't know it's true, that he played with Ferri Kepa. He was very old and invasive maybe, right? I sat in with the band he was playing. He was playing with the French band. He was working there with the French band.
Uh-huh.
At the jazz club. And I sat in and played a few songs.
Who else did you hear in France?

Yeah. I heard some French band like Claude Luther. And some bands I don't remember the name, so all of them were very bad anyway. There was one band who played like Hot Fives time in France, in Paris. Everybody knows about it. The guys you had here before, they probably know about it. Uh-huh. Because he's been playing for a long time, maybe ten years. They're actually not that good now, if they still existed. I don't know. But when I heard them, they wasn't that good. Like people told me they were before.
Uh-huh.

I know people from Sweden who have been there, I know I've heard them before. And I heard blues singers there. Like Champion Jack Dupree, who is from New Orleans too. Uh-huh. And I heard Memphis Slim from Chicago. And, uh, who else? Another piano player. Curtis Jones, also. These people I heard there.
Yeah, well he played with that Moguli Jospin band.
Yeah?
Curtis Jones, I think maybe not with him, but uh…
No, he probably not with him, yes.
In between and all.
Uh-huh, yeah. And he was up in Sweden and made a TV program there once.
Uh-huh. Yeah.
He made, but Mae Mercer too. In California I think she's a singer.
I don't know anything about her.
She was over in England with Keith Smith band for a while. Uh-huh. That's when I first met her.
Did you say you went to Belgium too? Yeah. Did you hear any bands there?

No, I never got an opportunity to hear any bands. I know there is clubs and there is bands in there. I went to a club but I never went into it. I left on, I wanted to hear a particular band but they weren't there at the time so I left. I never heard any bands. I know there is bands and I know they like music because these guys in Barry Martin's band, they've been over there and played a lot. I think Keith Thomas has been there with them too, in Brazil.
Where else did you hear bands in, in Europe?
London of course. All kinds of bands. London and I heard one band in Wales, in Cardiff.
Was it good?

Yeah, it was pretty good. Me and Mike Casimir was there, a drum player. We sat in with the band and played a little. It was good, I would say. And I was up in Scotland, we went up there with the band and played there.
What band was that?

That was a band, I don't know what they called themselves but Jim Young was the leader of the band. Bass player, he once played with Keith Smith. Half of the band is Scottish, half of it is English. They played at the pub on Drury Lane in London. I played with them there for two months, three days in a week. They went up to their hometown in Edinburgh, played on weekends. I was up there with them.
Well you played quite a bit professionally in England too then.
No, I didn't make any money.
Oh you just played with these bands just for fun?
Yeah.
You just played with Keith Smith for fun too?

Yeah, well a little. I thought I was, I intended to join the band maybe, to professional but I found out that professionally they didn't make very much money. The other thing was that people just leaving and coming to that band all the time. It's nice and they didn't play that well either. And finally Keith Smith got hurt, you know, in his eye. That was when I was there. So he wound up in the hospital. That was no use for me standing no more. So that's when I left.
Well he has a lot of trouble with men changing in the band, huh? Yeah.
He's changed recently, he's changed again since I was there. And there was no, nobody in the band was satisfied with it so I, I just didn't try to get into the band.
Yeah. Well what happened to his eye?

Well he, he, he's kind of a rough person, he always get in trouble. I don't know what's happened but it was in, in Soho one night. Uh huh. Yeah. Somebody, what's he put a dog on him, and bed him in his leg. Uh huh. He was there with his, one of his German friends. Uh huh. And they knocked him in the eyes or something like that. So he had, he, he, I, I went up to the hospital to see him. He was laying down with his leg up like this and his eye was all, stuff around his eyes. Uh huh. He had, had an operation. And he said it was going to be alright, he was going to have one more operation. Now I heard he's playing on one eye. Yes, that's what I've heard.
Yeah. I never ask him about it. Yeah. When I saw him, it's not the thing to ask him. Yeah. But I know what, I, I, I, I really believe that he was the one who made the trouble.
Cause I remember when playing with him once, he threw his chair on another person sitting out there in the audience, taking a chair like this. He's kind of making trouble.
But you must have played with some other bands besides Keith Smith. Yeah.

I played with that band at the pub I told you about, Kim Young's band. And I sat in in a lot of bands like Kid Martin's band, King Corley's band, and I can't remember all the names, but three different bands playing in pub, with Mike Casimir's band I played with.
Did you play with any brass bands? No.
What about Kim Corley?
What does he play like now?

Well, I, when I sat in with his band, it was really bad. He was very drunk himself. Couldn't do much. And the band played very soft. So you, you couldn't hear what it was doing really. But he changed members in the band since then. He's got, he didn't have a piano player at the time. Now Richard Simmons joined the band. He's got a piano player from there. And then, it's, I think it's changed a little. The band was very bad when I played with them. He didn't have no swing or nothing.
Well, how does he look? Does he look well?
Well, he doesn't look that bad with it. He's horribly drunk. Could hardly stand on it.
Tell me he looks a little yellow like John does.

Well, yeah, he, he looks a little, little, maybe a little sick. You can't see it too much because he has his big beard, you know. You can't tell how he really looks like. Anyway, that was the time when they started playing skiffle again. Went back playing Sam Revington, playing mandolin, guitar.
What about Mike Casimir's band? What's that like?
Well that was pretty bad when I was there. It's supposed to be quite good now. He's changed members in the band. He just started that band when I was there. When were you there?
What was last summer?
I was there about two months last summer. I lived with Mike Casimir in his apartment for a couple of weeks. That's why I know him so well.
Did he have Tony O'Sullivan on trumpet then?
No, Tony O'Sullivan was still here then I know. No, he's joining him now. The band is supposed to be very well from people like a very good band.
Who did he have on trumpet then? Joe Lied? No.
He was a fellow from out of town. He was not from London. He plays now with Jim Young's band. He was another guy who couldn't hold the band together. It was like Keith Smith. Mike? No, Jim Young.
Jim Young. Yeah. I see.
Mike's band is supposed to be good. I also read in the Melody Maker that I've seen him play in good places. That means that his band must sound quite well now. Like he played in Coilers Club.
Is Barry Martin any good?

No, not himself. He's not very good. Well, he swings all right but I mean what he's playing is very uninteresting. He's just banging his cymbal all the time. That's about all he does now. I guess he could play that. He doesn't. But are you some guys in his band who are very good musicians? Like the band you play is very good.
John Coles.
Yeah. He's good. I played a lot with him on kind of jam sets.
Back to New Orleans we were on the subject of the brass band and we never really got into that. You played yesterday.
Yeah. Oh the day before yesterday. Is it Monday today?
I think it's Monday.
Yeah, it was yesterday then. Yeah. It's gotta be Monday.
Yeah. What did you think of the band?

Oh I think it's pretty bad. I mean I enjoy more playing with the Rolf's brass band. Sounds more like the Eureka brass band or something like that. This band is too noisy and it's mainly because of Baptiste, which the awful trumpet player.
Well I had a hard time hearing you play your E flat a lot of times.
Well I had a hard time hearing it myself.
Yeah.

But it was all right after a while because this English trumpet player, Clive, he managed to outplay Baptiste a little bit. He played loud and that was the only way to get Baptiste to quit playing on a few choruses. So we managed to get him to play some other songs instead of singing the blues all the time. So it sounded a lot too bad. It sounded a lot better than the other time I played with him. It was about the week before. What was that, the Jolly Bunches?
Yeah. You played in Maryland I understand yesterday. Yeah. You told me and Betty Rankin told me she came to the parade.
Yeah. It was kind of hard for me to play that horn. It's the wrong system for me and the wrong keys and everything.
You play the beam system over there and that was an album. Yeah it was an album.
It was also so small. I never played before. It was small as it was hard to press the keys right.
Oh yeah. I see. What about the other trumpet players in the band? Oh, he's cheek.
He doesn't do anything. He has to walk around looking at the girls.
Maybe he's having a good time.

Oh yeah, he found a good one. That's great. And Andrew Anderson, he plays, you don't hear too much. He has such a soft tune. That's the reason why Gorman liked him so much. He liked that kind of soft. You don't hear too much from him but he's playing good though. Who else was, that was not a trumpet player. Yeah, Baptiste and his English player.
Alive Wilson.
Yeah, he played quite well I would say. And Manipole is the guy who does the best, keeps the band going best.
Yeah, he always seems to me to be working to help everybody. Oh yeah. Phil Ann is playing good.
Yeah. The Tormund players aren't very good. They're all right though. They aren't really bad but it's not very good.
Well I felt they weren't trying.
No, they never tried. Thea's going to make some sounds.
Yeah, I think they...
The tuba player was very good. Minor, is it? I know, yeah.
I felt the Tormund players, well I noticed Paul Crawford seemed to be clowning or something because he felt he couldn't do anything else, you know, with a band. Yeah, yeah.
Crawford, I don't like Crawford playing at all. Either with a regular band or with a brass band.
What band did you hear him with?
I heard him with Ray Buck and these guys. Punch Miller and the... Yeah, Punch Miller and the...
Johnny Weir.
Yeah.
That's Punch's band and I guess you heard him with some other bands.
Yeah, I heard him with Without Punch, the same band Without Punch. Yeah.
I don't know whose name they go under.
Oh, Johnny Weicks I guess, or Sweet Emma Bar, whoever is in the band. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, he doesn't sound very good to me. And the drums, we left out the drums of that band.
Yeah, yeah, it was pretty good this time.

It was two bass drums, two snare drums. Yeah. The day, the week before we only had one snare drum. Mm-hm. And the week before also Alan Jaffe was playing the tuba. Mm-hm. And then the rhythm session, they went out of the beat several times.
Jaffe doesn't have very good time? I don't know if it was Jaffe or whoever it was.
I thought he had good time. I think he, I don't think it was his fault.
I think it was the snare drum.

Mm-hm. But I don't think that the bass drum came out. He's a good drum man. Yeah, Bukka T, yeah. Yeah, he wouldn't get out of the beat. But this time it was good. There was two snare drums this, uh, Jaffe, Avid Jefferson. Andrew Jefferson and Noel Glass. Yeah, yeah. That was pretty good now.
Yeah. But still it's not a good brass band, I wouldn't say so.

They don't play together. They're just playing solo. Yeah. And then the bass drum, I don't think that the bass drum came out. Yeah. Yeah. I don't think that the bass drum came out. He's a good drum man. Yeah, Bukka T, yeah. Yeah, he wouldn't get out of the beat. I don't know what's really happened, but it's several times it happened like that.
But this time it was good. There was two snare drums this, uh, Jaffe, Avid Jefferson. Andrew Jefferson and Noel Glass. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah.

That was pretty good now. Yeah. And then the bass drum is not a good brass band, I wouldn't say so. They don't play together. They're just playing solos and stuff like that. Never get a chance. I mean, we had two saxophones and clarinet and the trombones. We could easily play together. These five musicians could play parts of the songs. Like I could play the melody and the saxophone play parts and the trombone play parts. They never stopped playing the trumpets. They play the trumpets all through. You never get the chance.
Well didn't they add another trombone later on?
Yeah, a fellow came in there, Shine or whatever they call it.
Yeah, Erwin Jones is real nice.
Yeah, he came in there and started playing. He sounds pretty good actually.
He likes progressive music.
Yeah, he really disliked when we started playing this rasp and some soul man. So don't play that dead music. You want to play when the sings, you know.
Clive said he sounds like album one and he talks about J.J. Johnson.
Yeah, he likes that kind of his life. I played a jam session with him, Rolf and I, and the Japanese drummer who was here before.
Yo.

Yeah. We played, had a session. Kimmy Rolf. Yeah, that's his name. We had a session together. That sounded not too bad. We played him well on some songs. But he actually, he don't know anything. I mean he don't know any tunes, he don't know anything about chords or nothing. He has feelings.
But did you ever play a funeral here? No.
I didn't. My friend did, Rolf did. Yeah.
And you saw some though?
Yeah, I saw quite a few.
What did you think about the funeral?

Oh yeah. Actually I think that I shouldn't go there for the first point. I had nothing to do with it, really. I think it's stupid for all the people who are going there, it has nothing to do with it. But I've been there a few times, because Rolf was playing the trumpet in the band. Like on the Yacht-Bilow play. I think the people should stay away from that. I mean if they're going to bury somebody they don't want a lot of tourists hanging around with cameras or drinking beer and fooling around. It's kind of a bad scene to me.
I think so too. It's awful. It's disgusting.
Yeah it is. It's a little bad. It was beautiful music though. Particularly George Williams was beautiful music.
I thought they played very well together. It was about eighteen pieces.

I was surprised it was so good. I mean it was just a mixed band, mixed up, all kind of people. It sounded very well. But that was when they played the hymn, when they played the song after that, that sounded
awful.
Yeah that was the best music. It was better than Eureka actually.

I never have understood what happened to the brass bands. The trouble is really in the trumpet players more than anything else. Yeah it is. Either they're lazy or else they want to play progressive in a different way.
Yeah they don't want to play the melody nice. They think that playing the melody nice that is like doing nothing.
That's very strange. You know because the other instruments are at least passable as a rule.
Yeah.
And the drummers aren't that bad. Who was the drummer the week before at the Jolly Bunch?
It was Pukatini's son.
Again.
Yeah. They play quite well together.
Well was that a nice quiet parade at the Jolly Bunch?
Oh I wouldn't say so but it wasn't that bad.
Was it as bad as the one this past Sunday? Last Sunday?
I was about to say what I was saying.
Young Men's Olympians huh? Yeah.
It was about the same. The week before the Jolly Bunch, I think it was the week before, maybe it was the Jolly Bunch, there was some shooting, some guns.
That's a Lady Zulu's.
Yeah that was Lady Zulu, that's right. Were you there?
No I left, I always leave those.
Yeah but only Jolly Bunch I remember was the guy chasing somebody else with the knife, like running after him. Yeah. There was a little fight, but it wasn't that bad.
Well it doesn't sound like fun to me though to get shot at.
No.
I left out of that.

No. I don't see the point really in these parades no more. It's the point of going around playing music while they're shooting each other. And the worst of all is that they play these bad songs all the time. Same. They aren't really bad but when they play them ten times it gets to be bad after a while.
What do you mean what song?
They play the blues, they play this da da da, da da da da da. They play that all the time on the show.
The second line.
Yeah.
The whooping blues where they all holler.
Yeah. They play that all the time and it's getting a bit dry. I would like to play some more real. I mean what I think is more parade songs.
What do you mean? What part?

Like when we played this Bugle Ball March. March or something like that. I think that fits in a lot better. And you also get the bands to play better if you play these songs because they don't know these songs so well. They can't play too many bop phrases on them. They stick more to the melody line because it's more complex. I guess that's the reason why they play the blues because if they play the blues they can't play anything on that. They know that they can play anything on it. They don't have to play brass things. Mm-hm. But D-John he like that stuff. He like to play the blues.
Well the people seem to like him.

Oh yeah. But this is time- he's really hard trying to get this brass band proper I think. Mm-hm. It seems like that- that's why he using bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo
bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo
Sheik don't like him. I know that Sheik don't like him at all. Sheik doesn't do anything on this place by the way. He has to walk in there. Hardly play anything.
When you heard the Eureka what were they like?
It was pretty good. Not great but pretty good. It was all over the river. Yeah. It was one funeral. It was pretty good.
Who did they have?

I don't remember all the guys. I didn't even know who they were when I was there. I remember Sheik and Henry was there. I think Sheik was with the band wasn't he? I think she was with the band. Sheik, Poesy.
Did they have Peter Bocca or whatever?
Yeah, he was one of them. I can't remember all the guys. I wonder if it wasn't Booker T playing?
Yeah, he used to play some of them. Yeah, Booker T was there too. Usually it's Booker T and Chester Jones. Yeah, Booker T and Chester Jones. Did you hear Earl Humphrey? Was he with them back here?
No. Well, I heard him once but I don't remember why it was. It probably was with Eureka.

Might have been. I wasn't there I don't think of course. I never go to the funerals across the river. There's just nothing but white people, you know. Yeah. I feel very bad. They make me self conscious white people.
Yeah. Standing outside the church waiting for them to come out and play some music for them.
Stick the camera down in the grave and everything. It's almost that bad.

It is. I feel kind of rotten going out there. Yeah. Yeah, it's so funny. Every time it's going to be a funeral it's spread out down the preservation hall. For all the tubers. So they can go down there.
I didn't ask you about the other Swedish bands though. I really talked about three or four of them at the most.

Yeah. You mean not strictly New Orleans bands? No, the New Orleans style ones. Yeah. But we have a band outside of Stockholm we have some bands too. Mm-hmm. We have a band in Helsingborg. I don't know if they exist no more but they used to have a band there playing New Orleans style. We have a band in Gothenburg. You probably know that town. It's a big town. Mm-hmm. Playing too. And Borås. Town where all the girls are. 80% girls in the town. 80% girls? I don't know how much it is but anyway it's a lot more girls than boys. Why is that? It's because they have these kind of factories you know. Only for women working or so.
Oh, I see.

And all the boys live in the town. We played there many times. It's our favorite place. Why? To play there. It's tremendous to play there. All the girls. Yeah, I've been there many times. They have a band there. And all kinds of bands they have. I don't know. A lot of these bands are very bad. I don't know them. They're low gas rockers. Do you know the names of any of them? Yeah. It's called Riverbould 46.
Where is that?

At Gothenburg. And in Borås it's called, uh, oh I even met one of the members here in New East. Borås band. I can't remember what it's called. But they try to adapt these New Orleans sounding names. Yeah, of course they do. And the only one who has another name is, is Rolfs band called, original Optimus orchestra. You know what Optimus is? Optimus? Optimus in Sweden is, is a, is a kind of a lock. A mark on a lock. A particular lock they have all over.
Oh yeah. It's a trade name for a lock. Optimus. Yeah. Yeah. Trade name.

Well they have a club here at all the Optimus. Yeah. That's kind of a good name if you figure out. Most of them are very bad names and stupid companies. They try to take everything and mix it all together. Yeah. They get everything you know, they want it to be like this. Yeah.
Well it's the same thing in England. The original Superior Paragon. That's crazy. Yeah, that's P. Minter's band.

Oh, he has that. Yeah. I even got the card for it. Does he play very well, B? I only heard him once. He was over here when I was there, see. He came back just before I left. Oh, I see. But he plays kind of, like he's not sure what he's doing or something like that to me. His brother though is a very good musician. His brother is the best drummer in London. Kay? Yeah. Kay Mountain. Very good musician. I really like him. He's better than Barry Martin? Oh yeah. A lot better than Martin. Maybe Martin could play that good if he tried but he doesn't try. He play with this Kay, he play with the Gothic band now.
That's a dance band. Oh, that's a jazz band. Yeah, well a jazz dance band, not a brass band.

No, no, no, no, not a jazz band. No, in Sweden there is not too many bands except for they have this more modern Dixie band. Like they have a band called Dixie Six, a band that existed for a very long time. They have this Storwell Creepers, a small band. Ralph Eklund, he's played 20 years or so. Still playing. It's very good. They have a band called The Lord too. They break up now. Okay, they have a pygmy jazz band. It doesn't exist no more. You know A. Taline, a trombone player? Modern trombone player is very famous now. He used to play with pygmy jazz band. He's one of the most modern musicians now. Yeah. That's the way it goes most of it Dixie Landbairn. Now there are so few clubs in Stockholm. Stockholm we only have one jazz club really now. It's called the Gasell Club. It's a very old club. It's from Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to Oakland to from the 40s. It's the only one who sticks to jazz all the time.
It's like England, they have a lot of the guys have changed from trying to play New Orleans style, then they're trying to play modern.

Yeah, but in England, yes, there is not so many modern musicians as in Sweden. They don't have so many modern guys. In Sweden there is a lot, there is a lot of modern musicians. They are very good too, tremendous good. They don't get no work, I mean like dance jobs. Only they can play is at some restaurants. They have a restaurant called the Golden Circle in Stockholm where all musicians from the States come, Pad Pau and all these guys, they play that.
Well they don't play for drinking, how much?

Well they do too there. That's both for eating and drinking. But we could never play for these kind of things. We only play for dancing and for our, kind of our own people, young people that are dancing. Not for drinking, never. The only time we played for drinking was in Denmark. And they don't have these kind of rules they have in Sweden.
Oh you have, you're like England, you have the jazz club there.
Yeah. Yeah.
You think that changes the music any?

Well, the music, it's kind of bad really. Because you can't do much besides playing or you know that. You don't have the same, like when we played in Denmark we really had the ball. That was really nice. You could drink, you could do whatever you want. You could do whatever you want to. It's kind of boring to play at the jazz club sometimes.
I see that we're just about out of tape. So I think we better stop.
Okay.
Alright, so thank you very much. I'm going to just let it run off now. And I'll get you to sign this release. Uh huh. So that I can pay you.

segments.chapter: Opening and Swedish background
segments.title: Opening of the interview and Lars Edegran's birth
segments.summary: Allen sets up the tape, date and place. Edegran gives his birth date and Stockholm as birthplace.

segments.chapter: Opening and Swedish background
segments.title: Family jazz background, piano lessons and instruments
segments.summary: His father played in a 1930s dance band and his brother played Dixieland; he took classical piano from age seven, taught himself the other instruments and began playing jazz at about 15.

segments.chapter: Opening and Swedish background
segments.title: His father's dance band and brother Tommy's Dixieland piano
segments.summary: He describes the 1930s dance repertoire of his father and his self-taught older brother Tommy, who quit in the late 1950s because of rock and roll.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: Why Swedish traditional players quit; audiences prefer the Beatles
segments.summary: Players quit when they marry because audiences are young and traditional jazz is only for dancing; young people like rock.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: Early Swedish jazz bands, Lindstrom and the Hepcats
segments.summary: Swedish jazz bands from the late 1940s, a singer named Britta, the Youth Jazz Calendar, trumpeter Jack Lindstrom and a recent Danish festival.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: His Imperial Band and Rolf's Original Optimus Orchestra
segments.summary: He names the members of his Stockholm band and the other traditional band he plays piano in.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: Style of his band compared with modern New Orleans playing
segments.summary: His band sounds like a Bunk Johnson band, unlike Rolf's more modern band or the Preservation Hall style.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: His first bands, with his brother and the Snakes
segments.summary: He first played irregularly with his brother, then a year with a modern Dixieland band.

segments.chapter: Playing in Sweden
segments.title: Favorite pianists, including Yancey
segments.summary: He explains his own piano influences and names Jimmy Yancey as his favorite; both men praise Yancey's simplicity.

segments.chapter: First weeks in New Orleans
segments.title: Arrival in New Orleans, Preservation Hall and Kid Thomas's band
segments.summary: He hitchhiked from Chicago, sat in at Preservation Hall and heard Kid Thomas's band, disliking pianist Charlie Hamilton at first.

segments.chapter: First weeks in New Orleans
segments.title: Other places heard: Preservation, Harmony and parades
segments.summary: He has been at Preservation almost nightly, played parades and sat in with Kid Sheik; the Harmony Hall was only dance music apart from one pianist.

segments.chapter: First weeks in New Orleans
segments.title: The recording session with Toshiki Hiramatsu
segments.summary: He describes a poorly rehearsed session with a Japanese drummer, its line-up, and why it went badly.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: Favorite bassists, saxophonists and clarinetists in New Orleans
segments.summary: He praises Sylvester Henry, John Handy and George Lewis, and discusses the tone and condition of various players.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: George Lewis's and Gorman's ideas about playing softer and slower
segments.summary: He agrees that bands should play more softly and slowly, dislikes Preservation Hall loudness, and recalls Gorman's planned band.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: Dixieland Hall and Kid Howard's playing
segments.summary: He has visited Dixieland Hall and finds Kid Howard plays only the melody.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: Red Garter band changes and George Lewis's group
segments.summary: George Lewis takes over the Red Garter, with a modern-sounding earlier band, a weak pianist and a better-sounding room.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: Rowdy audiences at the Red Garter
segments.summary: He calls the audience drunken and noisy, shouting for the Saints.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: Playing bass drum in a brass band
segments.summary: He played bass drum a couple of times in a brass band, once welcoming George Lewis at the airport.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, clubs and players
segments.title: New Orleans musicians visiting Sweden and money for traditional players
segments.summary: Few New Orleans bands tour Sweden, modern jazz is more popular, and traditional players earn little except on tours and in the country.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Tape change and Edegran's full name
segments.summary: Allen restarts the tape, and Edegran gives his full name and the date.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Hearing jazz in Germany, Paris and the rest of Europe
segments.summary: He lists countries visited, met a German pianist, sat in with a French band with an old New Orleans musician, and heard blues singers in Paris.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Blues singers in Europe and Belgium
segments.summary: Talk of Curtis Jones, Mae Mercer, and Edegran's failed attempt to hear a band in Belgium.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Playing in London with Jim Young and Keith Smith
segments.summary: He sat in around London, Wales and Scotland, played in Jim Young's pub band, and left Keith Smith's band after Smith was injured.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Sitting in with Kim Corley's band
segments.summary: He sat in with several London bands including Corley's, which was poor and its leader drunk.

segments.chapter: Playing and hearing music in Europe
segments.title: Mike Casimir's and Barry Martin's London bands
segments.summary: He lived with Mike Casimir, comments on his band and on Barry Martin's drumming, and praises John Coles.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: The weekend New Orleans brass band: horns and players
segments.summary: He judges the brass band he played in the day before, criticizing trumpeter Baptiste and praising other players.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Brass band personnel and rhythm section problems
segments.summary: Further comments on trumpets, trombones, tuba and drum section, and on why the band does not play together.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Trombonist Erwin Jones and a jam session with a Japanese drummer
segments.summary: A new trombone player joins, and Edegran recalls a jam session with Rolf and the Japanese drummer.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Watching a New Orleans jazz funeral
segments.summary: He disapproves of tourists at funerals while praising the music of a mixed band.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Parades, shootings and the repertoire of second-line bands
segments.summary: He criticizes violence at parades and the constant repetition of blues, wishing for real marches.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: The Eureka Brass Band and white spectators at funerals
segments.summary: He recalls hearing Eureka at a funeral across the river and both men dislike white onlookers.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Other Swedish traditional bands and the Optimus name
segments.summary: He names bands in other Swedish towns, explains the Optimus name and compares English band names and drummers.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Modern jazz in Sweden and England and the rules of jazz clubs
segments.summary: Sweden has many modern musicians but little work, the Golden Circle exists, and Swedish club rules ban drinking, unlike Denmark.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
segments.title: Closing of the interview
segments.summary: Allen ends the tape and asks him to sign a release.
